data.title: Taiwan's Stock Pickers Are Walking Out to Bet Their Own Money
data.description:
NEW YORK, Oct. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Fly On Wall Street News Commentary - Taiwan's benchmark stock index was up 62% this year, the best showing of any major equity gauge in the world, when Bloomberg reported on Oct. 16 that some of the island's professional fund managers and analysts are quitting their jobs to invest their own money. Strict rules keep them from trading the very stocks they pick for clients, and in a year when about one in ten stocks in the index has more than doubled, some have decided the trade-off is no longer worth it. Companies and funds mentioned in this article include: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company Limited ( TSM ) [TSMC] , ASE Technology Holding Co., Ltd. ( ASX ) [ASE] , United Microelectronics Corporation ( UMC ) [UMC] , iShares MSCI Taiwan ETF , The Taiwan Fund, Inc. ( TWN ) .

Watching From Behind the Locker

Taiwan does not ban personal investing outright, but its asset-management code of conduct bars staff from trading a locally listed stock or a linked derivative within seven business days before or after their firm's funds trade it, which in practice rules out personal stock-picking. Fund managers must also lock away their phones, laptops and smartwatches each morning until the market closes at 1:30 p.m. The phone rule was formalized in 2024 to deter insider trading, the Taipei Times reported in July, after six former fund managers from four firms were indicted for front-running trades through the accounts of relatives and friends.

Ken Tsai, 40, a fund manager who until July worked at a large Taiwanese asset manager that Bloomberg did not name, told Bloomberg he made a Taiwanese maker of AI-server data-transfer components his fund's largest holding in 2024. The stock rose more than fivefold in 2025 and about sixfold again this year, but he owned none of it personally. "It left me with a strong sense of relative deprivation," he said. He now works at a private investment firm in Taipei, which was also not named. Pay adds to the pull: Taiwan portfolio managers earn roughly US$124,000 to US$311,000 a year, well below Hong Kong base salaries, according to Bloomberg, citing headhunters and recruitment-firm data.

The private shops they are joining sit outside those rules. They register as private companies with the Ministry of Economic Affairs and do not need asset-management licenses from the Financial Supervisory Commission because they do not raise public money. Brokers told Bloomberg some of them now generate more than NT$10 billion in monthly trading volume, rivaling mid-sized asset managers.

The Rally Behind the Exits

Much of the rally traces back to the AI hardware supply chain. TSMC reported third-quarter revenue of NT$1.49 trillion (US$46.7 billion) on Oct. 15, up 50.9% from a year earlier, while net income jumped 68.7% and gross margin reached 66.4%. It guided fourth-quarter revenue from US$52.3 billion to US$54.3 billion.

Chip packaging and testing has ridden the same wave. ASE Technology ( ASX ) reported September net revenue of NT$88.1 billion, up 45.5% from a year earlier, and third-quarter revenue of NT$244.2 billion, up 44.8%.

Mature-node foundry UMC reported August sales up 30.71% from a year earlier, lifting year-to-date sales 14.66%. In its second-quarter report, the company guided for capacity utilization above 90% in the third quarter and said revenue from its 22/28nm business continues to set record highs.

CONTINUED... Read more market coverage at: flyonwallstreet.com

A Talent Squeeze, Not a Stampede

The numbers point to churn more than an exodus. Fewer than half of Taiwan's 20 largest local equity mutual funds have kept the same portfolio manager for more than three years, according to fund-data site MoneyDJ, and Bloomberg reported that applications for junior roles at some international firms have roughly halved this year. Yet the FSC said the industry's registered headcount actually rose to 4,729 in September from 4,581 at the end of 2025. Firms are responding: the largest foreign asset manager in Taiwan is offering cross-market analyst roles and office rotations to keep staff.

Regulators are paying attention. The FSC said on Oct. 15 it is gathering information and plans to review the rules, balancing market development against conflicts of interest and investor protection. One asset-management executive told Bloomberg there is no easy solution for now.

The Case for the Pros

At least one professionally managed fund has kept pace. The Taiwan Fund ( TWN ), a closed-end fund listed in New York, reported a 47.36% total return for its fiscal quarter ended May 31, against 26.12% for the TAIEX Total Return Index over the same period, with net asset value of US$116.90 a share at the end of that quarter.

Investors who prefer to own the whole market can use the iShares MSCI Taiwan ETF, which holds about US$11.9 billion in assets.

Last week was a reminder of how quickly the math can change. The TAIEX fell 4.6%, its first weekly decline in five weeks, as a technology selloff spread and TSMC CEO C.C. Wei warned of macroeconomic uncertainty and weak consumer demand, according to Trading Economics. In New York, TSMC's shares fell 8.98% from the Oct. 9 close to $412.61 on Oct. 16, ASE dropped 14.86% to $39.53, UMC slid 13.68% to $19.82, the iShares fund lost 7.04% to $106.26 and The Taiwan Fund ( TWN ) declined 8.78% to $94.18, according to Stock Analysis data. For the managers who just traded a salary for their own account, those swings now land on them.

data.title: Stora Enso publishes information brochure on the demerger process and Bergslagets Skogar as a standalone company

STORA ENSO OYJ STOCK EXCHANGE RELEASE 23 November 2026 at 9:00 EET

HELSINKI, Finland, Nov. 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Stora Enso has published an information brochure providing shareholders with additional information on the demerger process and Bergslagets Skogar as a standalone company.

As announced on 30 October 2026, the Board of Directors of Stora Enso Oyj ("Stora Enso" or the "Company") has approved a demerger plan (the "Demerger Plan") concerning the separation of Stora Enso's Swedish forest assets business through a cross-border partial demerger (the "Demerger"). Under the Demerger Plan, all assets, rights, debts and liabilities relating to, or primarily serving, the Swedish forest assets business would be transferred without a liquidation procedure to Bergslagets Skogar AB ("Bergslagets Skogar"), a Swedish public limited liability company to be incorporated in the Demerger. The Board of Directors of Stora Enso has proposed that the Extraordinary General Meeting, convened for 15 December 2026 (the "EGM") would approve the Demerger Plan and resolve on the Demerger as set out in the Demerger Plan, as well as on the other agenda items set out in the notice convening the EGM.

Stora Enso has today published an information brochure containing additional information for its shareholders on the demerger process and Bergslagets Skogar as a standalone company (the "Information Brochure"). The English-language Information Brochure and its Finnish translation are available on Stora Enso's website at storaenso.com/egm2026.

Overview of Bergslagets Skogar
Bergslagets Skogar would be an independent forest company headquartered in Falun, Sweden, owning and managing approximately 1.22 million hectares of land. Its business would comprise the ownership, management, and development of Stora Enso's forest land in Sweden and related forestry operations, the production of paints and colour pigments, and the management of renewable energy projects. The core commercial activity would be the sale of harvesting rights to industrial customers in the Swedish sawmill and pulp mill industry, complemented by external seedling sales, renewable energy land leases, selected land transactions, and income from land-use rights. Building on its long-term customer arrangements, the business model is designed to preserve long-term forest value while generating recurring cash flows with limited capital expenditure requirements.

Carve-out financial information on Bergslagets Skogar
The Information Brochure includes Bergslagets Skogar's unaudited combined financial statements as at and for the years ended 31 December 2025 and 2024, prepared in accordance with IFRS Accounting Standards as adopted by the EU, and its unaudited condensed combined interim financial information as at and for the nine months ended 30 September 2026, with comparative information for the nine months ended 30 September 2025, prepared in accordance with IAS 34 Interim Financial Reporting. This financial information has not been audited or reviewed by an auditor.

Selected carve-out financial information on Stora Enso
The Information Brochure also includes selected unaudited illustrative financial information for Stora Enso excluding Bergslagets Skogar for the financial year ended 31 December 2025 and the nine months ended 30 September 2026. This information illustrates the hypothetical effects of the Demerger on Stora Enso's consolidated income statements as if the Demerger had occurred on 1 January 2025 (including the September 2025 divestment of approximately 175,000 hectares of Swedish forest land) and 1 January 2026, respectively, and on its consolidated statements of financial position as if the Demerger had occurred on 31 December 2025 and 30 September 2026, respectively.

Completion of the Demerger and first day of trading
The planned date of registration of the completion of the Demerger is 31 March 2027, subject to, among other things, approval by the EGM. Trading in the shares of Bergslagets Skogar on the regulated markets of Nasdaq Stockholm and Nasdaq Helsinki is planned to commence as soon as possible thereafter.

  • 6 March 2026: Stora Enso presents executive management team for the new forest asset company
  • 8 January 2026: Proposed members to the Board of Directors of the new forest company planned to be separated from Stora Enso

For more information about the demerger, please visit the Demerger info page.


Bergslagets Skogar would be an independent forest company based in the heart of Sweden's forest economy. The company will be focused on creating long-term value from forests for our stakeholders, society and nature. Built on deep expertise based on science and advanced forestry practices, the company will manage its forests as living, evolving systems to support their resilience and productivity over generations. The company will continuously explore new ways for forests to contribute economically, socially and environmentally, from harvest rights and renewable raw materials to recreation, biodiversity and climate benefits, and other ecosystem services. bergslaget.com

Stora Enso is a global leader in renewable materials with a strong focus on packaging. Our purpose is to replace non-renewable materials with renewable solutions. Together with our customers, we design and deliver competitive, high-quality packaging materials and solutions, made from fresh and recycled fibers, accelerating the transition to a circular bioeconomy. data.title: US futures bounce as Asia scrambles to slow AI stocks rout
data.description:
SINGAPORE, Nov 23 (Reuters) - US stock futures rose on Monday while authorities in Asia readied to prop up sliding stock markets, after a wipeout last week for the tech and chip counters at the heart of the AI boom.

Investors are questioning whether the vast sums of mostly borrowed money spent building data centres to power AI tools will generate profits large and fast enough to repay lenders.

Last week's 10% drop in the Nasdaq was its largest weekly decline since pandemic panic gripped markets in March 2020, while the fall in Taiwan's chipmaker-heavy benchmark was the biggest since 1990.

On Monday, Nasdaq 100 futures bounced 3% in Asia and S&P 500 futures rose by 2%, while Taiwan stocks rose 2%, with government support helping to stabilise the market.

European futures were steady, and although the rout deepened for South Korea's KOSPI index, it lifted from a 10-month low to trade down by about 2.5% in the late afternoon.

The KOSPI was global equities' leading light in the first half of this year, as bets on chip demand more than doubled the index's value in six months.

In the reckoning, the index has halved from its peak, and South Korea's finance minister on Monday reiterated plans to stabilise the market, if necessary, which helped to steady shares.

Taiwan's financial regulator has ordered a tightening of short-selling rules for stocks, while in China, stock exchanges announced a batch of support measures such as easing requirements for margin financing.

"We need to be a bit careful here," said portfolio strategist Damien Boey at Wilson Asset Management in Sydney.

A suite of mood indicators he tracks showed US markets spent three sessions in "panic" territory last week, he said. That can sometimes signal the worst is over, but in this case traders might have a hard time finding a reason for a turnaround.

"If you don't have a policy pivot (at central banks) then there's no catalyst for a risk appetite panic to turn into a durable bounce," he said, leaving investors jumpy and unsure.

Japanese markets were closed for a holiday on Monday but futures indicated selling pressure, while markets in Hong Kong and China sank to new multi-month lows. Bonds and the dollar, safe-haven assets that rose sharply on Friday, mostly held gains.

AI TRADE TURNS

For about four years since the launch of chatbot ChatGPT, the "AI trade" has lifted a wide range of stocks, from chip to switch and cable makers to electricity generators on the assumption of explosive growth in computing demand.

According to analysts, AI spending is staying solid, with Morgan Stanley forecasting a rise next year in hyperscaler capital expenditure of more than 70% to top $1.6 trillion.

But the mood in the market has shifted drastically.

The exit of Jensen Huang, the Nvidia ( NVDA ) CEO nicknamed the "godfather of AI", has called the chipmaker's strategy of financing some of its customers into question. The faltering debut of AI leader Anthropic, which on Friday closed 8.5% lower on its first full day of trading, showed traders turning fickle.

Over the year to date, a Hong Kong index of AI stocks spanning Chinese chipmakers and AI companies is down nearly 60%.

The next test, besides the price performance of US markets this week, will be the results and outlook from computer maker Dell on Tuesday and, next month, whether the US Federal Reserve raises interest rates as investors expect.

The dollar's strength lifted it above 159 yen briefly on Monday, kept the euro below $1.10 and pinned the mood-sensitive New Zealand dollar near a 17-year low.

(Reporting by Tom Westbrook. Additional reporting by Liang-sa Loh in Taipei; Editing by Edmund Klamann, Jacqueline Wong and Jamie Freed)

data.title: Zhuanzhi Think TankZZZK Launches OPC Post-Level Agents and Knowledge Parts Library: The “One-Person Company” Moves from Legal Concept to Industrial Infrastructure
data.description:
Chengdu,China, Nov. 23, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- ZZZK today announced the official launch of the OPC post-level agent (One Person Capacity Agent), the knowledge parts methodology, and the Knowledge Parts Library. The core of this announcement is to move the “one-person company” beyond a legal label and toward industrial infrastructure that can be certified, assembled, and delivered: the OPC agent is a post-level agent that takes the post as its unit of delivery, covers the full closed loop of a job, and passes L4 “plug-and-play” certification; the knowledge parts methodology decomposes post knowledge into reusable, composable, and verifiable knowledge parts; and the Knowledge Parts Library provides standardized knowledge components for post-level agents, supporting rapid assembly and independent onboarding. ZZZK says this marks the transition of OPC from an individual entrepreneurial strategy into a new stage of enterprise organizational restructuring and macroeconomic measurement.

Image: https://ml.globenewswire.com/Resource/Download/583d9402-756f-4a0f-8452-56cfe7822bcb/1.jpg

Within the framework of ZZZK’s OPC Research Institute, the “one-person company” is no longer merely a legal label for sole proprietors or freelancers. It is a new organizational form for the digital age: the individual as the decision-making core, knowledge as the vehicle of output, and networks as the boundary of expansion. In the words of the preface to its white paper, a one-person company “is not ‘small’ in scale, but ‘sharp’ in decision-making, ‘specialized’ in assets, and ‘one’ in soul.” From this redefinition, ZZZK has built a complete chain of argument running from individual survival strategies to trillion-dollar economic forecasts and on to the restructuring of traditional enterprises.

2050: An Economy Measured in “Households.” 

The Global OPC Economy Development White Paper (2026), released in March 2026, was the first to systematically put forward the concept of the “OPC economy,” and it offered a startling forecast: by 2050, more than one billion people worldwide will work in the one-person company mode; OPCs will number one billion; and they will contribute 65% of global GDP, roughly 350 trillion US dollars. The penetration path is set at about 4% in 2026, 11% in 2030, 19.5% in 2035, and 65% in 2050 under the baseline scenario. The premise of this forecast is a redefinition of what a one-person company is: in the AI era it “has broken through the traditional legal definition to become a human-machine collaborative lean organization with AI as its productivity infrastructure and a single natural person or micro-team as its decision-making core.” One billion OPCs are not one billion legal entities but one billion economic units whose center is individual judgment and whose executing extremities are clusters of agents. The white paper also introduces GODI 1.0, the Global OPC Development Index, which assesses each country’s ecosystem along five dimensions: individual empowerment, policy support, factor supply, economic output, and social well-being.

Image: https://ml.globenewswire.com/Resource/Download/1cf04fb5-a8f7-4555-93a3-a6c342e0b6f4/2.jpg

The OPC Agent: A Post-Level Capability System. 

What underpins that forecast is ZZZK’s distinctive definition of the “OPC agent.” In common usage OPC stands for One Person Company; ZZZK reinterprets it, in the context of agents, as One Person Capacity Agent. It is not “an AI assistant that chats better,” but a post-level capability system that covers the full closed loop of a job, passes L4 certification, and carries a human-machine division-of-labor protocol. Its core question is not what AI can do, which is what general agents answer, but whether a given job can be handed to AI to run independently. To make “independent onboarding” measurable rather than rhetorical, ZZZK established an L1–L5 maturity certification. L4, “plug and play,” is the hard threshold for taking a post, with five criteria: full coverage of the post’s functions; accuracy of no less than 95% in high-frequency scenarios; contingency plans for edge cases; complete and traceable audit trails; and an automatic escalation mechanism. “Below L4, you are not on duty.” Methodologically it proposes a four-step path of job decomposition, OPC-ization, agentization, and business encapsulation, in which job decomposition is defined as “the step that decides whether the whole project succeeds,” requiring structured separation across four layers: knowledge, process, decision, and output. The accompanying CFDE five-step method, covering identification, extraction, structuring, injection, and verification, aims to turn the veteran’s “it depends” into live IF-THEN rules, case libraries, and decision trees, and to deposit them as reusable knowledge parts in the Knowledge Parts Library. The Knowledge Parts Library launched this time is precisely the engineering vehicle of this methodology.

The key consequence of this definition is that the OPC agent was never a “tool for one-person companies only.” It serves the job as the unit of delivery: a one-person company needs one person to run a post independently, while a traditional enterprise needs a post to be undertaken independently by an agent, with humans making the exception judgments. The same architecture is therefore both the infrastructure of individual entrepreneurship and the operating unit of corporate restructuring.

Image: https://ml.globenewswire.com/Resource/Download/abd3ef31-abc0-4899-b982-ca8f62fb2d47/3.jpg

OPC-izing the Traditional Enterprise: Tearing Down Department Walls, Building Self-Referential Units. 

On the enterprise side, OPC-ization does not point to layoffs or flattening. The diagnosis is that the real problem is not how many layers exist, but that functional departments “each carry only one link in the business loop.” Sales takes orders, R&D builds, service handles after-sales, and “no unit is accountable for the full customer result.” The solution is to break the enterprise into multiple OPC self-referential units, each holding a complete demand–process–delivery–feedback loop, deciding and allocating resources on its own, and answering for the final result. The five-step rollout runs as follows: map the value chain to identify independent loops; draw responsibility boundaries and appoint unit leaders; design standardized interface protocols between units; build an exception-management dashboard; and redesign profit sharing, with 30% to 50% of unit profit going to team bonuses. Disclosed figures include a 40% average shortening of delivery cycles, more than 300% growth in employee-initiated proposals, and a rise in change success rates from about 30% to 75%. At one 150-person software company split into 15 self-referential units, new-product launch time fell from six months to two, complaints dropped 60%, and attrition fell from 25% to 8%. On relations with external OPCs, ZZZK draws a clear line: OPC embedding is not outsourcing but “an extension of organizational capability.” Outsourcing means “do a project, deliver a result, then end”; embedding means “becoming part of the organization’s capability, collaborating and iterating continuously.” It sets out four roles, namely gap-filler, capability amplifier, new-business scout, and standard-setter, with this premise: internal capability is “reinforced concrete,” OPCs are “add-on modules,” and modules do not replace concrete but slot in when needed. Both sides gain: OPC founders find a sustainable niche, and enterprises fill, at variable cost, a capability gap where “hiring takes two to four months and skills go obsolete in twelve to eighteen.”

Image: https://ml.globenewswire.com/Resource/Download/7db4f843-97b6-4aea-8cd4-6e27d02b010f/4.jpg

Knowledge Parts Library, High-Energy Organizations, and the SOE Reform Pathway. 

ZZZK further stresses that the Knowledge Parts Library is the knowledge base of the OPC agent: it decomposes post knowledge into reusable, composable, and verifiable knowledge parts, which post-level agents can call on demand, assemble quickly, and pass L4 certification to achieve independent onboarding. Accordingly, the one-person company is further defined as a “high-energy organization”—not a small entity measured by headcount, but a high-energy-density organization with individual decision-making at its core, knowledge parts as assets, OPC agents as executing extremities, and networks as expansion boundaries. ZZZK proposes that this high-energy organizational form is the ultimate pathway for deepening the reform of state-owned enterprises (SOEs): SOE reform should not stop at optimizing departmental collaboration or cutting layers, but should decompose business loops into self-referential units that can be independently accounted for, decide autonomously, and answer for final results, using post-level agents and the Knowledge Parts Library to rebuild capability supply and organizational operation, so that the organization shifts from “departmental assembly” to “high-energy unit collaboration.”

A “Strong Proposition” Worth Taking Seriously. 

ZZZK’s OPC argument has a pronounced “strong proposition” style: 65% of GDP coming from one-person companies by 2050; agents delivered as posts rather than as tasks; and the right transformation for traditional enterprises being not better departmental collaboration but decomposition into self-referential units. Every one of these claims can be challenged and should be tested empirically. What deserves attention is not the precision of the numbers but the categorical shift the argument attempts: recoding the one-person company from a career choice into a basic grammar of industrial organization. When posts can be undertaken independently by agents, when the basic unit of the firm shifts from department to self-referential loop, and when the unit of economic measurement slides from enterprise to capability holder, what ZZZK is betting on is a whole set of definitional rights over work, organization, and value creation. Whether that definition earns enough institutional recognition and market validation before 2050 arrives will be the touchstone of the proposition’s ultimate worth.

data.title: Following the Launch of iPhone Duo, BENKS Introduces a New Kevlar® Case with Integrated Hinge Protection.
data.description:
Shenzhen,China, Nov. 23, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Apple's first foldable smartphone, iPhone Duo, officially arrived at Apple Store locations worldwide on October 23, 2026, following the opening of pre-orders on October 16. Its launch has brought renewed attention to the specific protection needs of foldable devices, including how to protect the hinge while preserving the phone's folding experience.

Responding to these requirements, BENKS has introduced the ArmorGrid Air Grand Combo with Hinge Protection for iPhone Duo, a three-piece protection set featuring a Kevlar® back case with dedicated hinge protection, a front frame case, and a tempered glass screen protector. The set also retains BENKS' ArmorKeys™ Camera Control Button, bringing hinge protection and everyday functionality together in one coordinated design.

Image: https://ml.globenewswire.com/Resource/Download/314efd1a-5dc3-4c63-8a8b-1a58091fe27a/benks1.png

A Dedicated Approach to Hinge Protection

Most protective cases are designed around the familiar vulnerable areas: the back panel, corners, and camera lenses. Foldable phones change that equation. Their hinges are constantly involved in the opening and closing experience, making them an important consideration in any protection strategy.

BENKS addresses this with a dedicated full-coverage hinge structure designed to shield against everyday scratches and impacts.

The real question for any hinge-protective case is how well it maintains that balance over time. Coverage is important, but so is preserving the natural folding experience.

ArmorKeys™ Maintains Access to Essential Camera Controls

Beyond hinge coverage, the new design retains BENKS' ArmorKeys™ Camera Control Button, addressing another practical consideration in protective case design.

Physical controls remain an important part of everyday smartphone use, particularly when accessing camera functions. Protective cases need to provide coverage without making these controls difficult to reach or operate.

ArmorKeys™ features a dedicated button designed to maintain access to the camera control function after the case is installed. Together with the integrated hinge-protection structure, it brings mechanical coverage and everyday functionality into the same design.

Image: https://ml.globenewswire.com/Resource/Download/72c1a2d3-9437-4e2e-9a9c-6997566aa380/benks2.png

Kevlar® Gets a More Expressive Finish

The ArmorGrid Air series continues BENKS' use of genuine licensed Kevlar® fiber, bringing its material approach into the new hinge-protection configuration.

Known for its strength-to-weight characteristics, Kevlar® is used as the exterior material of the back case. The choice supports the product's focus on protective construction while maintaining a relatively streamlined design.

BENKS also incorporates its Fluxure Weaving technique, featuring a geometric surface pattern inspired by diamond-shaped grids, sharp edges and clean lines.

Rather than treating the exterior as purely functional, the design gives the case a more distinctive visual identity through its woven texture.

The hinge-protection version is offered in Obsidian Black, Beyond Blue and Cherry Purple, providing different finishes within the ArmorGrid Air design language.

Image: https://ml.globenewswire.com/Resource/Download/a08d0501-f5c7-431b-ac17-2f34bc8445e8/3.png

A Three-Piece Protection Set for iPhone Duo

The ArmorGrid Air Grand Combo with Hinge Protection extends its focus beyond the hinge through a coordinated three-piece configuration.

The package brings together:

Kevlar® Back Case with Hinge Protection: Combines the ArmorGrid Air exterior with an integrated magnetic sliding hinge structure.

Front Frame Case: Adds coverage around the front of the device.

Air Shield Clear-Edge Screen Protector: Provides an additional protective layer for the display.

Other design details include a raised camera frame and precisely aligned cutouts intended to maintain access to the phone's functional areas. The overall configuration reflects the need to consider the front, rear, camera area and hinge as interconnected parts of a foldable device's protection requirements.

Explore the ArmorGrid Air Grand Combo with Hinge Protection in Cherry Purple.

Image: https://ml.globenewswire.com/Resource/Download/15347295-9911-4f10-8204-45bbb6a53b20/benks4.png

Rethinking Protection for Foldable Devices

The arrival of foldable smartphones brings new considerations to mobile accessory development. Hinge movement, magnetic alignment, folding clearance, and access to physical controls all play a role in how a protective case is designed.

With its latest ArmorGrid Air Grand Combo with Hinge Protection, BENKS brings these considerations together in a device-specific solution for iPhone Duo. By combining an integrated magnetic sliding hinge structure, Kevlar® construction, ArmorKeys™ Camera Control Button, and a three-piece configuration, the product reflects a more comprehensive approach to foldable phone protection.

data.title: United States: TotalEnergies Strengthens its Partnership with Continental Resources to Develop its Gas Production
data.description:
PARIS--(BUSINESS WIRE)--  

TotalEnergies has signed a new agreement with Continental Resources, under which TotalEnergies acquires interests in natural gas upstream assets. The transaction is expected to add approximately 150 MMscf/d1 (equivalent to around 26 kboe/d) to TotalEnergies’ net gas production in the United States by 2032.

“We are pleased to further expand our cooperation with Continental Resources, a leading U.S. operator in the region. This transaction will strengthen our natural gas production in the United States and consolidate TotalEnergies’ integrated position from Upstream gas production to LNG exports,” said Nicolas Terraz, President Exploration & Production at TotalEnergies.

TotalEnergies’ natural gas production in the U.S.

This transaction with Continental Resources builds on previous acquisitions of non-operated interests completed in 2025 in the Anadarko Basin with Continental Resources and in 2024 in the Eagle Ford play with EOG Resources and Lewis Energy. These assets will offer low-cost, low-emission, long-plateau production and are well connected to existing midstream infrastructure. Together with TotalEnergies’ operated Barnett asset, they are expected to bring the Company’s overall net natural gas production in the U.S. to approximately 850 MMscf/d2 (equivalent to more than 140 kboe/d) from 2032 onwards.

TotalEnergies’ LNG Activities in the U.S.

TotalEnergies is the number one exporter of U.S. LNG with 19 million tons exported in 2025, representing 18% of the whole U.S. production, out of which 14 million tons for Europe. The Company is integrated throughout the LNG value chain, with upstream gas production assets in Texas, Oklahoma and offshore U.S. TotalEnergies has invested in a number of major LNG projects in the U.S. including Cameron LNG and Rio Grande LNG. TotalEnergies also offtakes LNG from major U.S. terminals, such as Sabine Pass LNG, Freeport LNG, and Corpus Christi LNG.

data.title: Battalion Advanced Technology Ltd: Battalion commits up to £3 million to UK hypersonic materials programme with Oxford Sigma
data.description:
Programme SPEAR addresses three engineering problems that limit hypersonic flight. The intellectual property it creates will be owned by Battalion, a UK company.

LONDON, Nov. 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Battalion Advanced Technology Ltd ("Battalion") has signed a research agreement with Oxford Sigma Limited ("Oxford Sigma") to develop materials and component technologies for hypersonic applications. Programme SPEAR has up to £3 million committed over three years and will be carried out in the UK.

Materials performance is a critical challenge in hypersonic flight to enable better performance and capability. Heat, pressure and oxidation place demanding requirements on joints, seals and apertures. SPEAR focuses on three related engineering challenges: joining dissimilar materials, developing adaptive seals and creating windows that maintain their performance in extreme environments.

Oxford Sigma will carry out the research under Principal Investigator Dr Thomas P. Davis, drawing on its existing materials expertise and know-how. Battalion will own the intellectual property created through SPEAR and lead its commercialisation, with Oxford Sigma entitled to 1.5% royalties on qualifying future product sales and licensing income under the agreement.

Alongside new intellectual property, the programme aims to produce prototype hardware, supporting test evidence and manufacturing know-how, establishing a foundation for subsequent qualification and commercial development. Technologies will be assessed progressively, with investment focused on those offering the strongest technical and commercial potential.

Oxford Sigma brings together materials development, computational modelling, prototype manufacture and experimental testing within a single British-owned UK organisation. Its experience across fusion, nuclear and defence engineering enables the programme to consider manufacturing, verification and future qualification requirements from the outset, alongside materials performance.

The programme is designed to take technologies from early-stage research (Technology Readiness Level 2-3) to TRL 4-5, including the testing of prototypes and potential products under Battalion's direction. SPEAR will be coordinated with the hypersonic materials programme Battalion directs and funds at The Pennsylvania State University in the United States, and is aligned with AUKUS Pillar II, under which the UK, US, and Australia cooperate on advanced capabilities including hypersonics.

R. Michael Jones, Co-founder and Director of Battalion, commented:

"National security problems do not stop at borders, and the work on them should not either. SPEAR puts a British team on three of the hardest problems in hypersonic flight, alongside the programme we direct at Penn State. Allies attacking the same problem from different angles is how this moves quickly."

Dr Thomas P. Davis, Co-founder and Chief Executive Officer of Oxford Sigma, commented:

"Hypersonic flight and fusion energy share an opportunity: materials operating beyond the limits of conventional engineering. Our team has spent years developing materials and components for those conditions. SPEAR focuses that expertise on three defined materials themes, with a partner committed to taking the results towards practical applications."

About Programme SPEAR

Programme SPEAR is a research programme funded and directed by Battalion and carried out by Oxford Sigma over up to three years. It is staged, from research to prototypes and demonstrators, with progress reviews directing investment to the strongest technologies.

About Oxford Sigma

Oxford Sigma is a British-owned, internationally recognised advanced materials company based in Oxford, UK, focused on fusion, nuclear and defence systems. It is a supplier under the UK Ministry of Defence's Hypersonic Technologies & Capability Development Framework (HTCDF), with wider experience across UK defence research and weapons engineering programmes. Dr Thomas P. Davis, Co-founder and Chief Executive Officer, is Principal Investigator for Programme SPEAR. His background spans materials science, fusion engineering, defence materials, and materials standardisation. He holds a PhD (DPhil) in Materials Science from the University of Oxford.

About Battalion

Battalion Advanced Technology Ltd is a London-based company that develops hypersonic materials and wide-bandgap semiconductor devices for national security and dual-use applications. It directs and funds the underlying research at The Pennsylvania State University, ranked first in the United States for materials science research expenditures (NSF, FY 2024), and at Oxford Sigma in the UK through Programme SPEAR.

data.title: L&T Technology Services Launches SDVault.ai™ to Bring Engineering Intelligence to the Software-Defined Vehicle V-Cycle
data.description:
Highlights:

  • 250+ domain-aware AI agents, paired with deterministic automation and safety, cybersecurity and compliance guardrails
  • 12 interconnected engineering domains across the SDV V-cycle, from requirements to release
  • Early pilots indicate 30–40% additional engineering capacity

BENGALURU, India--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- L&T Technology Services (BSE: 540115, NSE: LTTS), a global leader in Engineering Intelligence Solutions & ER&D Consulting Services, today announced the launch of SDVault.ai™, an AI-powered engineering and assurance toolchain that helps automotive OEMs and Tier-1 suppliers accelerate the development, integration and validation of Software-Defined Vehicles (SDVs). SDVault.ai™ is part of LTTS’ EI for Engineering suite and is built on EIOne, the company’s Engineering Intelligence platform.

SDVault.ai™ brings Engineering Intelligence across 12 interconnected engineering domains, spanning requirements, system and E/E architecture, functional safety, cybersecurity, process assurance, software and code intelligence, verification, embedded debugging, virtual ECU validation, trace and network analysis, root-cause intelligence and regression and release assurance.

With more than 250 domain-aware AI agents, SDVault.ai™ combines AI with deterministic, rule-based engineering automation, particularly for safety-critical activities where repeatability, traceability and engineering control are essential. Engineers remain firmly in control of engineering decisions, verification and certification. SDVault.ai™ creates a connected engineering thread across the V-cycle, linking requirements and architecture with code, tests, failures, corrective actions and release evidence. This enables engineering teams to understand not only what changed, but what is impacted and whether the change has been adequately verified.

data.title: Omdia: Africa's Smartphone Shipments Fall 40% in 3Q26, With a Further 25% Decline Forecast for 2027
data.description:
LONDON--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Smartphone shipments in Africa fell 40% year-on-year (YoY) to 13.7 million units, down from 22.8 million a year earlier, according to Omdia’s latest research. This marked the steepest YoY decline in three years following three consecutive years of third-quarter growth. Rising component costs and currency pressures are changing how vendors price their devices and how consumers buy them across Africa's largest markets.

This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261122134076/en/

Rising prices weigh on smartphone shipments and market value

Shipments of smartphones priced below $100 fell nearly 70% YoY in 3Q26, while feature phone shipments grew 27%. Entry-level smartphones are becoming less profitable, prompting vendors to reconsider which models they offer and how they price them. Consumers who pay in cash, particularly those without access to operator subsidies or financing, are delaying upgrades or turning to refurbished smartphones and feature phones. Higher-priced smartphones are increasingly out of reach for these buyers.

“The figures show how affordability is shaping buying decisions in Africa. Some buyers are waiting longer to upgrade or choosing a refurbished smartphone to stay within budget,” notes Manish Pravinkumar, Principal Analyst at Omdia. “In many other regions, higher average selling prices (ASPs) helped sustain market value as shipments fell. In Africa, the ASP reached $222 in 3Q26, its highest third-quarter level in a decade. Even so, market value fell 15%. The increase in average price reflects a widening affordability gap and offers little evidence that buyers are moving to more expensive models.”

Nigeria and Egypt record the steepest shipment declines among Africa’s key markets

The size of the decline varied across Africa's key markets, reflecting differences in economic conditions, access to consumer financing, and exposure to currency and policy changes. Nigeria recorded the steepest decline among these markets, with smartphone shipments down 47% YoY. Fuel price pressures following subsidy removal, limited access to US dollars for import payments and higher handset costs further reduced household purchasing power.

In Egypt, smartphone shipments fell 41%. A weaker Egyptian pound and persistent inflation raised the cost of importing phones and manufacturing them locally, prompting consumers to delay upgrades.

In Kenya, smartphone shipments fell 35%. Shipments in the country’s core price segment, smartphones priced below $150, fell 44% as higher device prices put these devices beyond the reach of more buyers. Credit purchases and instalment plans are playing a growing role in helping consumers manage upfront costs.

South Africa recorded a smaller decline of 20%. Established operator distribution networks, contract upgrades, and a wider range of retail channels helped support shipments. High smartphone penetration, pressure on household budgets and longer replacement cycles continued to weigh on demand.

Samsung gains market share as TRANSSION retains the lead

TRANSSION accounted for 48% of smartphone shipments in Africa in 3Q26. Its shipments fell 43%, reflecting its exposure to the shrinking market for smartphones priced below $100.

Samsung recorded the smallest shipment decline among the five leading vendors, down 8%, and its market share rose to 23%. Its operator relationships and broad Galaxy A-series portfolio supported shipments. The Galaxy A07 4G and A17 4G together accounted for 56% of Samsung’s total smartphone shipments in Africa during the quarter.

Xiaomi’s shipments fell 49% as price increases across its portfolio weakened demand from channel partners and reduced its share of consumer spending.

HONOR’s shipments fell 14% YoY in 3Q26 after recording near triple-digit growth in the previous two years. Its performance in South Africa and expansion into other African markets supported that earlier growth. The decline shows how higher handset prices can slow even fast-growing vendors.

OPPO’s shipments fell 69% as it reorganized its operations as part of its integration with realme.

Tax reforms and device financing offer potential routes to recovery

Omdia expects smartphone shipments in Africa to end 2026 down 23% YoY and forecasts a further 25% decline in 2027.

“The forecast shows how heavily Africa's smartphone market depends on affordable devices and continued growth in shipments,” said Pravinkumar. “With cost pressures expected to persist into 2027, vendors face a difficult pricing challenge. They need to keep entry-level devices profitable, but passing higher component costs on to buyers risks putting smartphones beyond the reach of more households.”

Tax policy and access to financing will also shape the prospects for a recovery. Morocco reduced its smartphone import duty from 17.5% to 2.5%, illustrating how tax reform can ease cost pressures. Vodacom has introduced prepaid handset financing across all its African markets. In Nigeria, vivo is working with Credit Direct on device financing. M-KOPA continues to expand its smartphone financing model.

Pravinkumar added, “Governments, manufacturers and mobile operators all have a role in improving affordability. Closer cooperation will be essential to expand local manufacturing, make distribution more cost-effective, and give more customers access to financing. The next phase of growth depends on making connected devices affordable for a wider range of buyers.”

data.title: Analysis-Citi's $35-billion UK error could complicate exit from US regulatory penalty box
data.description:
NEW YORK, Nov 23 (Reuters) - An error that caused Citigroup to underestimate its risk-weighted assets by $35 billion, forcing it to inject capital into a UK unit, could complicate a long-running effort to exit a US regulatory penalty that has been a drag on its operations, experts said. 

While the misstatement happened in an overseas unit, it could raise questions for US regulators over whether Citi's penalties, or consent orders, from the regulators should be speedily lifted, said some analysts and former regulators. 

The orders cover regulatory demands to fix risk management, data governance and other problems and they date back to 2020, leading to costly fines and distractions for Citi. Reuters was first to report the $35-billion error on Thursday, citing a person familiar with the matter. "It's not a huge error given the size of the bank, but any misstep is going to complicate their efforts to escape their consent order," said Sheila Bair, a former head of the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. "As a general matter, I think this just reinforces the unreliability of models in setting risk-based capital requirements." 

While the error could complicate reaching the goal, it is unlikely to completely derail the bank getting the consent orders lifted, some analysts said. 

Citi Chief Executive Jane Fraser has said that exiting the consent order was her top priority, and she appeared to be nearing that goal.

Last month, Reuters reported that as recently as this summer, the bank was targeting the end of this year, or the first quarter, to submit the needed paperwork to regulators that could lead to the bank being able to conclude its remediation efforts, which have forced the bank to hire tens of thousands of additional employees. 

HIGHER BAR

The third-largest US bank has been aiming to present a comprehensive audit to the Federal Reserve and Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, so it will not hit any delays in approval, Reuters previously reported. 

"With the event in question occurring during a time period that overlaps with Citi's own attestation work regarding remediation efforts to lift the consent order, it could plausibly lengthen the duration for the 'sustained effectiveness' test, but it would be unlikely to reset the process," said Austin Taggart, a banking analyst at Morningstar.

As part of the consent order, regulators have ordered Citi to attest that data that it uses to file its required regulatory disclosures is correct and will be in the future.

Wells Fargo analysts led by Mike Mayo said in a note to clients that the mistake was not material from a regulatory perspective but that Citi suffered from having made mistakes in its past. 

"The perception is not great since the bar is higher for Citi after its prior mistakes," Mayo said.  

Citigroup said on Thursday it ​had identified and resolved an internal capital modeling issue at a European trading subsidiary this summer. "The subsidiary remained fully compliant with regulatory minimums throughout, with no impact on ​the holding company or main operating bank," it said.

On Friday, Citi declined to comment on any potential impact on prospects for its consent order.

On the question of whether this would create a setback for Citi resolving its consent order, the Federal Reserve declined to comment. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency did not return a request for comment. 

REGULATORY HEARTBURN 

While small in relation to Citi's firm-wide financials, the misstatement was more than 20% of the total risk-weighted assets in Citigroup Global Markets Ltd (CGML), the UK-based international brokerage operation where the error occurred, which had $155 billion as of the end of 2025, according to Reuters calculations based on regulatory filings. 

Risk-weighted assets are central to regulatory reporting, because they determine how much capital a bank has to hold in order to absorb losses. At issue is how and when banks use internal models to measure risk or standardized models developed by regulators. In many cases, banks need approval from regulators to use internal models.

The UK unit used an internal model to determine the riskiness of assets that had not been approved by regulators for some trades, people familiar with the matter have told Reuters. When the error emerged and the trades were plugged into the correct model, the measure of risk the unit was taking shot up and Citi was not holding enough loss-absorbing capital, they said.

Some experts said that even though the error happened in the UK, it will still be a concern in Washington.

"The first order of this is that it is a UK problem, but Citi is a US holding company so I would expect this issue to be reflected in the Federal Reserve's oversight of the US holding company," said Jeremy Kress, an associate professor of business law and a former Fed regulatory attorney. 

"The first order is that this is a big screw-up, but the second order is that if they are screwing that up, what else are they missing, which is what will really give regulators heartburn."

(Reporting by Stephen Gandel and Saeed Azhar; additional reporting by Pete Schroeder; editing by Megan Davies, Elisa Martinuzzi and Jonathan Spicer )

data.title: German automakers face winter of discontent as union battles loom
data.description:
FRANKFURT/LONDON, Nov 23 (Reuters) - Germany's automakers face months of contentious labour talks and strikes over job cuts and potential factory closures as the model that underpinned the country's highly paid auto workforce breaks down.

For years, strong earnings from global markets helped offset Germany's high labour and production costs, analysts say. But Chinese competition, US tariffs and weaker demand are undermining the profits that made that possible.

Volkswagen, Mercedes-Benz, Bosch and Schaeffler have responded with plans to cut thousands of jobs, curb investment and potentially close plants, moves likely to trigger fierce resistance from workers.

Andrew Bergbaum, a partner at consultancy AlixPartners, said declining investment returns and profitability point to a "difficult winter" in labour negotiations.

Volkswagen last month posted its biggest operating loss in more than a decade, while Mercedes-Benz and BMW saw their nine-month auto profit margins drop to 1.9% and 3.5%, respectively, down from 14.9% and 8.7% four years ago.

"They (unions) are in a very difficult place because companies aren't making any money, they're not investing any money, and management are increasingly bullish on trying to push through change," Bergbaum said.

FOCUS ON VOLKSWAGEN AND IG METALL TALKS

The tensions are most visible at Volkswagen, Europe's biggest automaker, which starts crunch talks on Tuesday with IG Metall, Germany's largest union, over fresh job and salary cuts. IG Metall has vowed fierce resistance to the company's demands.

Thorsten Groeger, the union's chief negotiator for wage talks with the company, said it was "out of the question" that an agreement could be reached this year as Volkswagen's offer was an insult to workers.

At €65 ($71) an hour, German auto workers are the world's highest paid, earning over one-and-a-half times more than their US counterparts and more than three times as much as workers in Poland, according to the Kiel Institute for the World Economy.

Volkswagen has said deep cost cuts are needed to remain competitive.

It aims to finalise a plan for its European factories by the end of June 2027, including a roadmap for four German sites the automaker says have no planned successor vehicle models.

The sites could be repurposed for military use, assigned vehicles for the Chinese market, or - failing other options - closed in the next decade, the company has said.

IG Metall has threatened strikes at Volkswagen from January 1 if no agreement is reached. One-day strikes have already hit BMW and Volkswagen's Audi division.

"We have to make sure we overcome the current tsunami in the sector and that companies do not go insolvent in the medium term. The IG Metall (union) must know this, too," said Daniel Bauer, head of Germany's SdK investor protection association.

The pressure extends beyond automakers. Europe's automotive suppliers will, on average, see their operating margins dwindle to 2.9% this year, down from 7.1% in 2018, a steeper fall than the decline to 5.8% from 9.0% at Chinese rivals, according to research from Roland Berger and Lazard.

"This is not just another downturn for European suppliers," said Roland Berger partner Felix Mogge. "Another round of cost cutting is simply not enough."

The industry's difficulties are also reflected in German jobs data.

Germany's auto sector workforce has fallen to the lowest level in at least 21 years, according to the federal statistics office.

"The fact is for Germany's car industry, there are going to be more job losses or fewer jobs created, however you look at it," said Ian Henry of consultancy AutoAnalysis.

DEEPER RESTRUCTURING AHEAD

Tesla's announcement last week of a €3 billion expansion of its plant near Berlin, four days after Mercedes-Benz said it would suspend German investments, underscored the contrast between established automakers and newcomers.

German automakers are producing fewer vehicles at home as overseas sales decline. Foreign sales fell nearly 8% between 2023 and 2025, according to data from industry lobby group VDA and the German statistics office.

Marco Santino, partner at management consultancy Oliver Wyman, said further cuts were likely, with automakers targeting more structural solutions and "not just these progressive layoffs that are going to reduce capacity, but probably not really solve the problem".

($1 = 0.9121 euros)

(Reporting by Christoph Steitz and Nick Carey; Additional reporting by Giulio Piovaccari and Rachel More; Editing by Emelia Sithole-Matarise)

By Sukanya Mitra

Nov 23 (Reuters) - Gold regained some ground on Monday after falling to a 14-month low last week, with investors weighing the deep selloff in US equities against upcoming US inflation data for fresh clues on the trajectory of interest rates.

Spot gold climbed 2.4% to $3,616.51 per ounce by 0530 GMT. Bullion fell about 9% last week, its steepest weekly decline since March.

US gold futures gained 2.9% to $3,616.60.

"The selloff in tech stocks and the expectations of weaker economic activity because of the weaker AI boom have led the markets to reprice the path forward for US interest rates, which has provided gold with some fundamental support," said Kyle Rodda, senior financial market analyst at Capital.com.

Traders are currently pricing in a 93.5% chance of a rate hike at the Fed's policy meeting in December, down from about a 100% probability last week, according to CME's FedWatch tool.

Lower odds of higher rates reduce the opportunity cost of holding bullion, enhancing the appeal of the non-yielding asset.

"Despite a modest rebound in early trading today, we still need to be cautious to call a bottom in gold. We also cannot rule out further forced liquidation if volatility in equity markets persists," said Dilin Wu, research strategist at Pepperstone.

US stock futures rose while authorities scrambled to shore up sliding stock markets in Asia, after a wipeout last week for the tech and chip stocks at the centre of the AI boom.

Fed Governor Lisa Cook made a case for more rate hikes on Friday, saying the Fed's current policy rate was not high enough to deal with inflation levels she viewed with "great concern."

Market participants now await the US Personal Consumption Expenditures data due on Wednesday, a key gauge closely watched by the central bank as it targets a 2% inflation rate.

Spot silver climbed 3% to $42.41 per ounce, platinum gained 1.2% to $1,314.85 and palladium rose 1.2% to $903.15.

data.title: MORNING BID EUROPE-AI, caramba!
data.description:
A look at the day ahead in European and global markets from Rae Wee

It's been a bruising November for the AI faithful, with markets from Taiwan and South Korea to the US staring at steep monthly losses as the selloff in tech and chip stocks at the heart of the AI boom shows little sign of letting up.

Investors are questioning whether vast sums of mostly borrowed money spent building data centres to power AI tools will generate returns fast enough to repay lenders or big enough to justify some of the high stock prices.

data.title: Analysis-Europe's cloud sovereignty push gains ground, but US hyperscalers remain dominant
data.description:
Nov 23 (Reuters) - A drive to ensure critical digital services can operate under European control is gaining traction, industry executives say, with governments and regulated industries taking sovereignty into account when awarding cloud services contracts.

While digital sovereignty has been a political objective for years, procurement criteria and contract awards are beginning to reflect those priorities.

The change follows a year in which European policymakers and businesses have become more sensitive to their dependence on US technology. US President Donald Trump's return to office and restrictions on access to some technologies heightened concerns over strategic dependencies, while cloud-service disruptions highlighted the risks of concentrating critical services with a small number of providers.

In April, the European Commission awarded four sovereign-cloud contracts worth up to €180 million ($198 million) over six years to groups led by Luxembourg's Post Telecom and Belgium's Proximus, alongside Germany's StackIT and France's Scaleway.

The Dutch government also signed a framework agreement with StackIT, saying it would reduce dependence on non-European suppliers and strengthen digital resilience.

Recent procurements by organisations including Denmark's state railway operator DSB, Swiss federal entities and Germany's public broadcasters have incorporated digital sovereignty requirements aimed at reducing dependence on individual providers and foreign jurisdictions.

"The sovereignty criteria are something that comes much more to the forefront in the public sector and then the leading regulated industries," said Markus Noga, chief technology officer at IONOS, Germany's largest hosting and cloud provider.

The shift is not always a choice between European and US providers. Google Cloud's S3NS joint venture with Thales, which has obtained France's SecNumCloud certification for handling sensitive government and regulated-industry workloads, was selected under the European Commission's €180 million programme.

Google Cloud said public-sector tenders increasingly assess providers on operational autonomy, control of encryption keys and cloud-exit provisions, which allow customers to move applications and data to another provider if required, rather than simply where data is stored.

"The true value comes from not being subject to a kill switch and being able to continue your operations indefinitely," Noga said.

Christine Knackfuss-Nikolic, chief sovereignty officer at Deutsche Telekom's IT services arm T-Systems, said digital sovereignty had shifted from a discussion topic to a procurement consideration during 2025.

She cited concerns over strategic dependence and operational resilience, including the temporary loss of access to Microsoft ( MSFT ) services by the International Criminal Court and restrictions on some AI model exports.

Recent European Commission initiatives, including its proposed Cloud and AI Development Act aimed at boosting Europe's cloud and AI infrastructure, have reinforced the trend.

Google said regulations such as the EU's Digital Operational Resilience Act, which sets technology-risk standards for financial firms, and NIS2 cybersecurity rules were prompting customers to scrutinise more closely who controls their data, cloud operations and critical technology infrastructure.

Nextcloud, which develops a self-hostable alternative to Microsoft ( MSFT ) 365, said demand for its software had increased roughly fivefold since the start of Trump's second term, while T-Systems said demand for its sovereign-cloud offering had risen more than fourfold since mid-2025.

Yet interest in sovereignty has so far translated into relatively few large-scale migrations away from incumbent providers.

A June European Commission draft of the proposed Cloud and AI Development Act said the market share of EU cloud providers had fallen from 29% in 2017 to 15% in 2022 and had remained stagnant since then, while Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud controlled more than 70% of the European cloud market.

THE LOCK-IN PROBLEM

Despite growing demand, providers say migration from incumbent platforms remains slow.

"The business still lags behind," said IONOS public-sector strategist Mark Neufurth.

He said only a single-digit percentage of discussions with public-sector customers currently result in contracts, while procurement reviews and migration concerns often stretch projects across 12 to 24 months.

Many organisations remain deeply tied to Microsoft Office ( MSFT ), Microsoft ( MSFT ) 365 and existing cloud infrastructure.

Google said customers increasingly sought cloud-exit strategies and open standards to reduce dependency on individual providers.

"The problem is that a lot of people don't like change and are afraid of migration projects," said Nextcloud Chief Executive Frank Karlitschek.

Amazon Web Services, Microsoft ( MSFT ) and Google have responded with sovereign-cloud offerings of their own. AWS said it conducted a test in October demonstrating that its European Sovereign Cloud could operate independently of infrastructure outside the European Union.

Microsoft ( MSFT ) pointed to partner-operated projects including Bleu in France and Delos Cloud in Germany.

Even companies benefiting from the trend acknowledge that a complete break with US platforms is unlikely in the near term.

"For large companies, for example, it doesn't make sense to migrate all workloads, only the sensitive ones," Knackfuss-Nikolic said.

Swiss banking software company Temenos said sovereign data and cloud initiatives were not yet mature enough for many large banks with international operations.

"We start to have pretty much all the pieces of the puzzle around Europe," said Sami Pienimäki, chief executive of Finnish software and device maker Jolla. "But it's damn difficult for a regular European, or even an educated policymaker, to see all those pieces on a table and make a clear picture."

($1 = 0.9108 euros)

(Reporting by Emanuele Berro in Gdansk and Hakan Ersen in Berlin, additional reporting by Paolo Laudani; Editing by Matt Scuffham and Sharon Singleton)

data.title: China stocks hit 16-month low as US chip curbs, rout in AI shares sour mood
data.description:
(Updates prices; adds quotes, details)

SHANGHAI, Nov 23 (Reuters) - China's share benchmark hit 16-month lows on Monday, led by tech stocks, as moves to ease margin trading requirements failed to reassure investors rattled by a deepening selloff in global AI stocks, fresh US chip curbs and a stuttering domestic economy.

Friday's Wall Street slump also dampened sentiment across Asia, while the prospect of additional US interest rate hikes threatened to tighten global liquidity.

The yuan steadied, though China's corporate bond market remained under pressure after weeks of volatility.

Measures unveiled over the weekend to support the market - including easing requirements for margin financing - are "inadequate" against the backdrop of a global stock selloff, said Wang Yapei, fund manager at Zijie Private Fund.

"The bearish stock market is eroding people's wealth and curbing consumption."

The benchmark Shanghai Composite Index fell 1% in morning trade, piercing the key 3,500-point level and hitting the lowest since early July 2025.

The blue-chip CSI300 Index lost 0.6% while Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index declined as much as 1.8% to the lowest level in 19 months.

China's semiconductor industry index slumped 5% following Friday's Wall Street tumble as a global selloff in chip and AI stocks deepened.

CHIP CURBS

Adding to the pressure, President Donald Trump said on Friday the US would penalise American companies that build data centers overseas, in Washington's latest move to restrict Chinese access to advanced US chips.

Trump's threat "further hit investor confidence in the global build-out of computing power at a time of closer scrutiny over AI expenditure," said Yuan Yuwei, hedge fund manager at Trinity Synergy Investments.

Recent US moves to close loopholes allowing China access to high-powered US chips - including restrictions on advanced AI chip exports to several Southeast Asian countries - have also pounded shares of Chinese AI companies hungry for computing power.

Hong Kong's Hang Seng Tech Index, which includes cloud service providers Alibaba ( BABA ) and Tencent ( TCTZF ), as well as AI model developers Z.AI ( KATJF ) and MiniMax ( MNMXF ) , hit 26-month lows on Monday and is on track for a nine-day losing streak.

Wu Qidi, director of Yuanda Information Securities Research Institute, said higher US Treasury yields had also knocked down China and Hong Kong tech stocks.

"The recent slide in Hang Seng Tech was partly driven by money flowing back to the United States."

YUAN STEADY, BONDS UNDER PRESSURE

Prospects of further US rate hikes have bolstered the greenback, with the dollar index hovering near a 20-month high on Monday.

China's onshore yuan was steady on Monday, changing hands around 6.6743 per dollar at midday. The currency has gained nearly 5% this year against the dollar.

Guotai Junan Futures said upward momentum in the yuan had been weakened by the stock market fall.

"The continuous weakness in Chinese stocks has dimmed the appeal of yuan assets" and triggered capital outflows.

In the corporate bond market, signs of financial stress in state-owned developer Huafa Group, which triggered market volatility in late October, continued to keep investors on edge.

China's bond exchange-traded funds (ETFs) remained under selling pressure on Monday, following weeks of turmoil.

(Reporting by Shanghai newsroom; Editing by Jochelle Mendonca and Jacqueline Wong)

data.title: Exclusive-Like SpaceX, Anthropic ran an unusual IPO process, chafing some bankers
data.description:
NEW YORK, Nov 22 (Reuters) - For the second time this year, Wall Street bankers and lawyers took home a massive paycheck from a record-setting initial public offering. And for the second time this year, some of them came out of it complaining in private about how the process was riddled with complications and unlike any they had worked on before.

With SpaceX's IPO in June, in which banks earned half a billion dollars in fees, bankers chafed over how tightly the Elon Musk-led company controlled the months-long process and kept financial and other information private, making it hard for advisers to do their jobs. 

As Anthropic's IPO, dubbed internally "Project Lantern", eclipsed SpaceX on Thursday and bankers took home more than half a billion dollars in fees, several people close to the process listed a litany of problems that had plagued the offering process: a compressed timeline, marred by last-minute changes and delays in sharing financial projections; rushed document approvals; and highly unusual restrictions on bankers and concern about leaks - especially after Reuters reported many details from a draft IPO filing weeks before it was made public.

Anthropic, for example, instructed some of its 22 IPO underwriters to limit the number of bankers working on the deal to four, asking the firms to make sure they were senior staff, several people familiar with the matter said. One of the people said the restriction likely came out of fear that information would leak, and that the banks found a way to work around it anyway. 

Underlying these complaints is a new power dynamic between technology companies and Wall Street. Companies such as SpaceX, Anthropic - and potentially also OpenAI in the future -  have come to wield enormous power as the transformative potential of artificial intelligence creates a frenzied demand for their shares, and they are wielding it to do things their way. That is upsetting some bankers. But banks and investors appear to have little choice but to play along.

"These companies certainly did have some market power to tell underwriters that it's not going to be business as usual," said Jay Ritter, a University of Florida professor emeritus who researches IPOs. "But the big Wall Street firms, I suspect, are still going to be doing things as business as usual for all but maybe OpenAI (after these two deals)."

Ritter added that both SpaceX and Anthropic had negotiated to pay underwriters nothing on the additional shares sold through the greenshoe option. "I don't think most companies are going to be able to demand zero spread on overallotment shares," he said.

Anthropic, Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley ( MS ), the two lead underwriters on the two IPOs, declined to comment.

SpaceX and OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment.

Both SpaceX and Anthropic debuted successfully, raising record amounts of money, and their shares rallied initially. A key part of the underwriters' job is to market the securities. Thanks to the demand for AI, that was an easy sell - both companies had order books oversubscribed many times over. 

After an initial burst in shares, the trajectories of the two big AI firms diverged. SpaceX climbed to a post-listing peak of $201.80 on June 16 before retreating below its $135 IPO price for the first time in mid-July. Anthropic's shares closed down 8.5% on Friday after a 17% first-day pop, as a dramatic unraveling of the AI trade showed that even a blockbuster listing could not shake the gloom hanging over the sector.

UNUSUAL NON-COMPETES AND RESTRICTIONS

In the case of SpaceX's IPO, the people close to the process said Musk's team dictated terms at every stage. Musk's team told the largest and most powerful US banks - including Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley ( MS ) - how to market SpaceX's stock and to whom. It told some banks the specific order sizes they needed to "fill" - in some cases a few billion dollars - and gave them instructions on what types of investors to bring. Banks signed on to underwrite the IPO without being told what they would be paid, the people said.

The underlying current running through Anthropic's IPO process was what several of the people who spoke to Reuters interpreted as a sense of extreme caution.    

Anthropic asked some senior officers at banks working on its IPO to sign legal documents restricting core members of the transaction team from working with rival companies, including OpenAI, Cursor, DeepSeek and Hugging Face, for six months after it went public, according to the people. 

Banks routinely manage conflicts and protect client confidentiality. But bankers and lawyers said it is rare for an IPO to impose exclusivity this broad, particularly on individual bankers. 

In previous head-to-head IPOs such as those of ridesharing rivals Uber ( UBER ) and Lyft ( LYFT ), or real estate companies Trulia and Zillow ( ZG ), banks could simply pick a side, in part because the deals were smaller and required fewer banks. 

Anthropic, by contrast, needed a broad syndicate to raise the enormous amount of capital it was seeking. That, some of the people said, explained why Anthropic sought to bind individual bankers with these restrictions. 

One banker who declined to sign on to the agreement said it was a challenge to find people who could promise not to actively cover or engage with Anthropic's peers, especially as several of those companies pursue their own initial or secondary offerings.  

INFORMATION LEAKS AND LATE NIGHTS 

Some of the restrictions were meant to control leaks of information. 

Nearly four weeks before Anthropic's filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission, called Form S-1, was made public, Reuters reported on it, revealing details of the company's financials, risk factors, dealings with other tech companies and other information. 

Anthropic also used a product called NetRoadshow to share information, instead of regular PDFs, with most of the banks underwriting the deal. 

NetRoadshow logs access details, including information such as who has seen the document and looked at which page. Documents on NetRoadshow also had individual bankers' names as watermarks. 

Leaks continued to surface in the press, but using NetRoadshow complicated bankers' work, including because the platform would not let them save copies of documents, one of the people said.

Anthropic planned to file an updated securities filing, called an S-1A, with the SEC with the price range and to launch the marketing on November 10. To do so, it needed to send a draft to all the banks in its syndicate for them to sign off on it.

The night before it was to happen, a law firm on the deal sent a PDF to the banks about the sale of shares in Canada. But soon it followed with another email asking them to disregard it, saying it "contains incorrect price range and share information," according to the email, which was seen by Reuters.  

The correct S-1A was then sent via the NetRoadshow platform around 2 a.m. New York time. Banks were told they had several hours to sign off on it before it was filed with the SEC. 

(Reporting by Echo Wang and Milana Vinn in New York; Editing by Paritosh Bansal, Jonathan Spicer and Muralikumar Anantharaman)

data.title: METALS-Copper sinks below $12,000 as jitters over AI, rate hikes eclipse tight supply
data.description:
Nov 23 (Reuters) - Copper fell below the $12,000 mark for the first time since March before recovering in early trade on Monday, as investors grew jittery over the outlook for AI and further rate hikes in the US, despite a still-tight spot supply.

Benchmark three-month copper on the London Metal Exchange rose 0.66% to $12,240.50 a metric ton as of 0330 GMT on Monday, rebounding after hitting $11,948 earlier in the session.

The most-active copper contract on the Shanghai Futures Exchange fell 0.82% to 95,250 yuan ($14,265.39) a ton.

Copper, widely used in the construction of AI data centres, has been caught in a sharp selloff since last week as investors question whether returns from massive spending on the technology will materialise quickly enough to justify the investment.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite slumped 10% last week, its biggest weekly decline since March 2020.

Markets are also betting on a US Federal Reserve rate hike in December and further tightening next year. The dollar remained near a 19-month high, making greenback-priced metals more expensive for buyers using other currencies.

Yet signs of spot physical tightness persist in China. While the LME cash-to-three-month copper spread has flipped into contango, with cash copper trading at a discount to the three-month contract, contracts on the Shanghai Futures Exchange remain in steep backwardation.

Spot premiums also indicate tightness in supply. The Yangshan premium , a gauge of Chinese buyers' appetite for imported copper, continues to set records, while the domestic premium also stayed strong at 5,800 yuan a ton on Friday, down from a record 7,250 yuan on Thursday.

Stocks in SHFE monitored warehouses rose , posting their first inflow in more than a month, but did little to cool premiums.

On the LME, aluminium gained 0.65%, nickel rose 0.78% and tin advanced 1.07%, while zinc slipped 0.04% and lead edged down 0.05%.

On the SHFE, aluminium climbed 1.69%, while zinc fell 0.97%, lead declined 0.38%, nickel slipped 0.23% and tin lost 0.20%.

($1 = 6.6770 Chinese yuan renminbi)

(Reporting by Dylan Duan and Lewis Jackson; Editing by Jochelle Mendonca)
